title: Logic circuits
examples: How do I draw an AND gate?
What is the difference between a half and full adder?
Can you show me how these gates work together?

explain.say: Today we are looking at logic circuits in computer science. These circuits use simple gates to make decisions. We will learn about the basic shapes of these gates.

items: AND Gate: Output is 1 only if all inputs are 1
OR Gate: Output is 1 if any input is 1
NOT Gate: Output is the opposite of the input

explain.say: The AND gate needs all inputs to be true for the output to be true. Think of it like needing two keys to open a lock.

draw.text: AND Gate: A AND B = Output

explain.say: The OR gate gives a true output if at least one of its inputs is true. It is like needing one key out of two to open a gate.

draw.text: OR Gate: A OR B = Output

explain.say: The NOT gate simply reverses the signal. If the input is one, the output becomes zero, and vice versa.
A half adder adds two single bits of binary numbers. It produces a sum and a carry out bit. For example, adding one and one.
A full adder adds three single bits of binary numbers. It takes two bits and a carry from a previous stage. This helps add larger numbers.

items: Inputs: A, B, and Carry In (Cin)

faq.q: What does 'binary' mean when we talk about these circuits?
faq.a: Binary means using only two digits, which are zero and one. These represent off or on, or false or true.
asks: What are the digits used in binary?
What does 0 and 1 represent in logic?

faq.q: Do I need to know the symbols for all the gates?
faq.a: You should know the standard symbols for AND, OR, and NOT gates. These shapes are universal in digital electronics.
asks: What do the gate shapes mean?
Are there different symbols for the gates?
How do I draw an OR gate symbol?

faq.q: How does a half adder actually add numbers?
faq.a: It adds two single bits, A and B. The sum goes to one output, and the carry goes to another output.
asks: What is the job of the half adder?
If I add 1 and 1, what do I get?
Does the half adder need a carry input?

faq.q: When do I need to use a full adder instead of a half adder?
faq.a: You must use a full adder when you are adding numbers that have a carry from a previous column. This is common in multi-digit addition.
asks: When is a full adder necessary?
What is the difference in inputs?
Does a full adder handle the carry?

faq.q: Can these gates be used to build a calculator?
faq.a: Yes, absolutely. By connecting many of these gates together, engineers build complex circuits like adders and eventually full processors.
asks: Are logic gates used in computers?
Can I build something big with these gates?
What is the connection between gates and CPUs?

facts: Logic gates process binary signals, which are represented by 0 and 1.
The AND gate output is only high (1) when all inputs are high (1).
A half adder adds two single bits and produces a sum and a carry.
A full adder adds three single bits: two inputs and a carry-in.

quiz.say: If the inputs to an OR gate are 1 and 0, what is the output?
quiz.why: The OR gate outputs one if any input is one, so 1 and 0 gives 1.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the output of a single gate is only one bit.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the gate must produce a clear binary output.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the OR gate is true if at least one input is true.

quiz.say: What is the output of a NOT gate if its input is 1?
quiz.why: The NOT gate always reverses the signal, so 1 becomes 0.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the gate functions perfectly with binary inputs.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the NOT gate must change the signal.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the output is always a single bit.

quiz.say: To add the number 11 (binary) and 1 (binary), which adder do you use?
quiz.why: Since you are adding bits and need to account for a carry, you need the full adder.

wrong.0: An OR gate only checks if any input is one, it does not perform addition.
wrong.2: An AND gate only checks if all inputs are one, it does not perform addition.
wrong.3: A half adder cannot accept a carry input from a previous stage.
